    #Part (iv)

    For Process A, find the work done by the system, and the heat transferred to
    the water. How is heat transfer related to the entropy change of the process?

    Work done by system,

    WA​=m(PΔv)=m⋅P(v2​−v1​)

    WA​=2(400)(0.53434−0.001084)

    WA​=426.6 kJ

    Using first law for closed systems,

    Q−W=mΔu=m(u2​−u1​)

    QA​−426.6=2(2647.2−604.22)

    QA​=4513 kJ

    Heat transfer into the system increases entropy change.

    #Part (v)

    For Process B, find the net work input for the process.

    Using first law for closed systems,

    Q−W=mΔu=m(u2​−u1​)

    −500−Win​=2(2553.1−604.22)

    Win​=−4397.76 kJ

    Work input to drive the paddle wheel.

    Work output of piston,

    Wout​=m(PΔv)=m⋅P(v2​−v1​)

    Wout​=2(400)(0.46242−0.001084)

    Wout​=369.07 kJ

    Net work input for process,

    Wnet​=369.07−4397.76

    Wnet​=−4028.7 kJ

    #CA3 S1 (2023 - 2024)

    In a crank-driven supercharger engine, the power to the supercharger comes mechanically
    from the engine’s crankshaft via a belt, gear, shaft, or chain. A supercharger increases the
    pressure of the air-fuel mixture and supplies it at a higher pressure to the engine. The
    greater mass flow rate provides more oxygen to support combustion in the engine.

    Given an ideal Otto 2-stroke cycle with a crank-driven supercharger. The engine cylinder
    volume is     0.02m3 and has a compression ratio of 10. The air is at 300K and 90kPa
    at the beginning of the supercharger. After the supercharger compression process,
    the air pressure is     200kPa. The maximum temperature of the cycle is 2000K.

    Assume the supercharger compression process is an isentropic process.
    Use cold-air standard assumptions:

    • cp​=1.005 kJ/kg⋅K
    • cv​=0.718 kJ/kg⋅K
    • R=287 kJ/kg⋅K
    • k=1.4

    (a) Plot the T-v diagram for the Otto cycle, including the supercharger.

    (b) Determine the air temperature after the supercharger compression process.

    (c) Determine the temperature and pressure after the expansion process.

    (d) Determine the heat added per unit mass during the combustion process.

    (e) Determine the net work with and without the supercharger.

    (f) Determine the thermal efficiency with and without the supercharger.

    (g) Determine the mean effective pressure with and without the supercharger.

    #Part (a)

    PT
    090 kPa300 K
    1200 kPa376.88 K
    25023.77 kPa946.68 K
    310613 kPa2000 K
    4422.51 kPa796.21 K

    #Part (b)

    Using the isentropic relations of an ideal gas,

    T0​T1​​=(P0​P1​​)kk−1​

    300T1​​=(90200​)1.41.4−1​

    T1​=376.88 K

    #Part (c)

    Using isentropic relations of an ideal gas,

    T1​T2​​=(V2​V1​​)k−1=(P1​P2​​)kk−1​

    376.88T2​​=101.4−1=(200P2​​)1.41.4−1​

    T2​=946.68 K

    P2​=5023.77 kPa

    Heat addition process is an isochoric process.

    v2​=v3​

    P2​RT2​​=P3​RT3​​

    5023.77946.68​=P3​2000​

    P3​=10613 kPa

    Using isentropic relations of an ideal gas,

    T3​T4​​=(V4​V3​​)k−1=(P3​P4​​)kk−1​

    2000T4​​=(101​)1.4−1=(10613P4​​)1.41.4−1​

    T4​=796.21 K

    P4​=422.51 kPa

    #Part (d)

    Using the first law for process 2-3,

    qin​=cv​(T3​−T2​)

    qin​=0.718(2000−946.68)

    qin​=756.28 kJ/kg

    #Part (e)

    Using the first law for process 4-1,

    qout​=cv​(T1​−T4​)

    qout​=0.718(376.88−796.21)

    qout​=−301.08 kJ/kg

    Net Work without Supercharger

    wnet​=qin​−qout​

    wnet​=756.28−301.08

    wnet​=455.2 kJ/kg

    Net Work with Supercharger

    wnet​=qin​−qout​−cv​(T1​−T0​)

    wnet​=455.2−0.718(376.88−300)

    wnet​=400.0 kJ/kg

    Alternatively, net work without supercharger is,

    wnet(w/o)​=cv​(T3​−T4​)−cv​(T2​−T1​)

    wnet(w/o)​=0.718(2000−946.68)−0.718(946.68−376.88)

    wnet(w/o)​=455.2 kJ/kg

    Alternatively, net work with supercharger is,

    wnet(with)​=cv​(T3​−T4​)−cv​(T2​−T0​)

    wnet(with)​=0.718(2000−946.68)−0.718(946.88−300)

    wnet(with)​=400.0 kJ/kg

    #Part (f)

    Thermal Efficiency without Supercharger

    ηth​=qin​wnet​​

    ηth​=756.28455.2​

    ηth​=0.60189=60.2%

    Thermal Efficiency with Supercharger

    ηth​=qin​wnet​​

    ηth​=756.28400​

    ηth​=0.5289=52.9%

    #Part (g)

    Using the ideal gas law,

    P1​v1​=RT1​

    v1​=2000.287(376.88)​

    v1​=0.54082 m3/kg

    From compression ratio,

    vmax​=0.54082 m3/kg

    vmin​=0.054082 m3/kg

    MEP without Supercharger

    wnet​=MEP(vmax​−vmin​)

    MEP=0.54082−0.054082455.2​

    MEP=935.21 kPa

    MEP with Supercharger

    wnet​=MEP(vmax​−vmin​)

    MEP=0.54082−0.054082400​

    MEP=821.80 kPa

    #CA3 S1 (2025 - 2026)

    #Question 1

    What is your understanding about gas turbine performance?
    Why is a good understanding of engine on- and off-design
    performance important for marketing and sales engineers?

    • Performance relates to how efficiently a gas turbine converts fuel into work
    • On-design performance — operation at the design point (optimal conditions)
    • Off-design performance — operation in the real-world (sub-optimal conditions)
    • Recommend gas turbine with expected performance under real-world conditions

    #Question 2

    Plot a clearly labelled T-s diagram of a simple turbojet engine.
    Determine the turbojet’s thrust specific fuel consumption.
    Assume all processes to be isentropic.
    Assume pressure thrust is zero.

    Atmospheric ConditionsPa​=60 kPa and Ta​=261 K
    Flight SpeedVa​=220 m/s
    Compressor Pressure Ratio16
    Air Mass Flow Ratem˙a​=53 kg/s
    Combustor Outlet Temp.T=1473 K
    Air Propertiescp​=1.005 kJ/kg⋅K and γ=1.4
    Gas Propertiescp,g​=1.147 kJ/kg⋅K and γg​=1.333
    Heating Value of FuelQHV​=48×106 J/kg

    Diffuser

    Temperature at diffuser outlet,

    T0,2​=T0,1​

    T2​=T1​+2cp​V1​2​

    T2​=261+2(1005)2202​

    T2​=285.08 K

    Pressure at diffuser outlet,

    T1​T2​​=(P1​P2​​)γγ−1​

    261285.08​=(60P2​​)1.40.4​

    P2​=81.713 kPa

    Compressor

    Pressure at compressor outlet,

    P3​=16(81.713)

    P3​=1307.4 kPa

    Temperature at compressor outlet,

    T2​T3​​=(P2​P3​​)γγ−1​

    285.08T3​​=161.40.4​

    T3​=629.51 K

    Combustor

    Energy balance,

    Q˙​=m˙ΔH

    m˙f​QHV​=(m˙a​+m˙f​)h4​−m˙a​h3​

    m˙f​QHV​=(m˙a​+m˙f​)cp,g​T4​−m˙a​cp​T3​

    m˙f​(48×106)=(53+m˙f​)(1147)(1473)−53(1005)(629.51)

    m˙f​=1.2095 kg/s

    Turbine

    Temperature at turbine outlet,

    Wturb​=Wcomp​

    (m˙a​+m˙f​)(h4​−h5​)=m˙a​(h3​−h2​)

    (m˙a​+m˙f​)cp,g​(T4​−T5​)=m˙a​cp​(T3​−T2​)

    (53+1.2095)(1147)(1473−T5​)=53(1005)(629.51−285.08)

    T5​=1177.9 K

    Pressure at turbine outlet,

    T4​T5​​=(P4​P5​​)γg​γg​−1​

    14731177.9​=(1307.4P5​​)1.3330.333​

    P5​=534.24 kPa

    Nozzle

    Temperature at nozzle outlet,

    T5​T6​​=(P5​P6​​)γg​γg​−1​

    1177.9T6​​=(534.2460​)1.3330.333​

    T6​=682.17 K

    Exhaust velocity,

    T0,5​=T0,6​

    T5​=T6​+2cp,g​V6​2​

    1177.9=682.17+2(1147)V6​2​

    V6​=1066.4 m/s

    Thrust produced by turbojet,

    T=(m˙a​+m˙f​)V6​−m˙a​Va​

    T=(53+1.2095)(1066.4)−53(220)

    T=46149 N

    Thrust specific fuel consumption,

    TSFC=Tm˙f​​=461491.2095​

    TSFC=2.6209×10−5 kg/N⋅s

    Using the ideal gas equation,

    Pv=RT

    P=vRT​

    Substituting the above into the 1st relation,

    T ds=du+P dv

    T ds=du+vRT​ dv

    T ds=cv​ dT+vRT​ dv

    ds=cv​TdT​+vR dv​

    ∫12​ds=∫12​cv​TdT​+R∫12​v1​ dv

    s2​−s1​=cv​ lnT1​T2​​+R lnv1​v2​​

    A polytropic process is defined by Pvn=Const.

    wpoly​=∫12​Cv−n dv

    wpoly​=C[−n+1v−n+1​]12​

    wpoly​=−n−1C​(v2​1−n−v1​1−n)

    wpoly​=−n−1Cv2​−n​v2​+n−1Cv1​−n​v1​

    wpoly​=−n−1P2​v2​​+n−1P1​v1​​

    wpoly​=−n−11​(P2​v2​−P1​v1​)

    Using the ideal gas law,

    P3​=P2​

    T2​T3​​=v2​v3​​

    Q−W=mΔu=mcv​(T2​−T1​)

    Q−(0−Win​)=0

    Q=−450 kJ

    Note that process A is an isothermal process.

    Using the first law for process B,

    Q−W=mcv​(T3​−T2​)

    Q=2(1.005−0.287)(120−300)

    Q=−258.48 kJ

    #Part (d)

    Process A is an isothermal process.

    T2​=T1​

    RP2​v2​​=RP1​v1​​

    v1​v2​​=P2​P1​​

    v1​v2​​=0.1

    Using entropy change equation from Part (b),

    s2​−s1​=cv​ lnT1​T2​​+R lnv1​v2​​

    s2​−s1​=0.287 ln(0.1)

    s2​−s1​=−0.66084 kJ/kg⋅K

    Alternative equation for entropy change,

    s2​−s1​=cp​ lnT1​T2​​−R lnP1​P2​​

    s2​−s1​=−0.287 ln(10)

    −0.66084=27+273−450/2​+sgen​

    sgen​=0.089158 kJ/kg⋅K

    #Part (e)

    Specific volume at state 3,

    v3​=0.4(0.0861)=0.03444 m3/kg

    A polytropic process is defined by Pvn=Const.

    P3​v3​n=P1​v1​n

    (v1​v3​​)n=P3​P1​​

    (0.8610.03444​)n=1000100​

    n⋅ln0.8610.03444​=ln1000100​

    n=0.71534

    Reversible polytropic work of an ideal gas,

    wpoly​=−n−11​(P1​v1​−P3​v3​)

    wpoly​=−0.71534−1100(0.861)−1000(0.03444)​

    wpoly​=181.48 kJ/kg

    Using the first law for process C,

    q−w=cv​(T1​−T3​)

    q−181.48=(1.005−0.287)(300−120)

    q=310.72 kJ/kg

    Entropy change of process C,

    s1​−s3​=cv​ lnT3​T1​​+R lnv3​v1​​

    s1​−s3​=(1.005−0.287)ln120300​+0.287 ln0.034440.861​

    s1​−s3​=1.5817 kJ/kg⋅K

    Entropy balance for process C,

    Δssys​=Tsurr​q​+sgen​

    1.5817=300310.72​+sgen​

    sgen​=0.54598 kJ/kg⋅K

    Since entropy generation is more than zero, process C is irreversible.

    #Question 3

    #Part (a)

    A Carnot power cycle consists of:

    • Isentropic compression
    • Isothermal heat addition
    • Isentropic expansion
    • Isothermal heat rejection

    Isothermal heat transfer is difficult to achieve as it requires
    large heat exchangers and it would take a very long time.

    #Part (b)

    Internal combustion engines are modelled as a closed cycle. However, in reality,
    it is an open cycle as there is a flow of air and fuel into the engine, and exhaust
    gases out of the engine.

    #Part (a)

    Regeneration increases the thermal efficiency of the cycle as heat addition process occurs over a smaller temperature range since steam enters the boiler at a higher temperature.

    For an open feedwater heater, steam extracted from the turbine mixes with the compressed liquid from the pump. Thus, extracted steam must be at the same
    pressure as the compressed liquid.

    For a closed feedwater heater, steam extracted from the turbine does not mix with
    the compressed liquid from the pump. Thus, extracted steam can be at a different pressure. However, the heat exchange process is not as efficiency.

    #EST S2 (2022 - 2023)

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    Let state 0 be the state before the partition wall is removed.
    Let state 1 be the state after the partition wall is removed.
    Let state 2 be the state once equilibrium is reached.

    Specific volume, work done, and heat transfer

    Specific volume of nitrogen,

    P0​v0,B​=Rs​T0​

    v0,B​=200.297(60+273)​

    v0,B​=4.94505 m3/kg

    Specific volume of vacuum,

    v0,A​=21​v0,B​

    v0,A​=21​(4.94505)

    v0,A​=2.4725 m3/kg

    After the partition wall is removed,

    v1​=v0,B​=4.94505 m3/kg

    P1​=P0​=20 kPa

    T1​=T0​=60°C

    Piston undergoes compression to maintain pressure equilibrium of 20kPa
    with the surroundings. Thus, the volume of the system after the partition
    is removed is equal to the volume of the nitrogen gas initially.

    Work done during compression process,

    w=PΔv=P(v1​−v0,B​)=0

    Note that there is no work done since initial and final volumes are the same.

    Since the system reaches equilibrium with the surroundings, T2​=227°C.

    After the system reaches equilibrium,

    P2​v2​=Rs​T2​

    v2​=200.297(227+273)​

    v2​=7.425 m3/kg

    Note that pressure is constant at 20kPa since the piston is free moving.

    Using the first law of thermodynamics,

    Q−W=ΔU

    Q=ΔU+W

    Q=ΔH

    Heat transfer from surroundings,

    q=Δh=cp​ΔT

    q=1.039(227−60)

    q=173.513 kJ/kg

    Work done by piston,

    w=PΔv=P(v2​−v1​)

    w=20(7.425−4.94505)

    w=49.599 kJ/kg

    Alternatively, heat transfer can be obtained using,

    q−w=Δu=cv​ΔT

    q−49.599=(1.039−0.297)(227−60)

    q=173.513 kJ/kg

    Absolute volume, work done, and heat transfer

    Heat transfer is 10 kJ more than work done by piston, thus Q−10=W.

    Mass of nitrogen gas,

    q−m10​=w

    173.513−m10​=49.599

    m=0.080701 kg

    Initial Vacuum Volume

    V0,A​=mv0,A​

    V0,A​=0.080701(2.4725)

    V0,A​=0.19953 m3

    Heat Transfer from Surroundings

    Q=mq

    Q=0.080701(173.513)

    Q=14.003 kJ

    Work Done by Piston

    W=mw

    W=0.080701(49.599)

    W=4.0027 kJ

    #Part (b)

    Entropy change of system,

    ΔSsys​=m(cp​ lnT1​T2​​−Rs​ lnP1​P2​​)

    ΔSsys​=0.080701(1.039)ln60+273227+273​

    ΔSsys​=0.034081 kJ/K

    Note that the second term is zero since P2​=P1​.

    Entropy change of surroundings,

    ΔSsurr​=Tsurr​Q​

    ΔSsurr​=227+273−14.003​

    ΔSsurr​=−0.028006 kJ/K

    Note that the surroundings lose heat to the nitrogen.

    #Part (c)

    Entropy balance for a closed system.

    ΔSsys​=ΔSsurr​+Sgen​

    0.034081=−0.028006+Sgen​

    Sgen​=0.062087 kJ/K

    Since Sgen​ is positive, the process is irreversible.

    #Question 4

    #Part (a)

    Given the same design operation specification, how does the
    ideal jet propulsion cycle differ from the ideal Brayton cycle?

    • Jet cycle has additional devices — diffuser and exhaust nozzle
    • Turbine work is solely used to power compressor, where Wtur​=Wcomp​
    • Efficiency is determined by propulsive efficiency rather than thermal efficiency

    #Part (b)

    How is the RPM of an actual 4-stroke petrol engine related to the number
    of thermodynamic cycles when compared to a 2-stroke petrol engine?

    A 4-stroke engine rotates twice for every one thermodynamic cycle.
    A 2-stroke engine rotates once for every one thermodynamic cycle.

    Description of 4-stroke engine:

    • Crankshaft rotates half a revolution during intake phase
    • Crankshaft rotates half a revolution during compression
    • Crankshaft rotates half a revolution during expansion
    • Crankshaft rotates half a revolution during exhaust phase

    The additional revolution comes from the intake and exhaust phases,
    which are not represented on the     T-s diagram of the power cycle.

    #Part (c)

    Given a mixture of several gases of identical masses for each gas, will all
    the mass fractions be identical? Will the mole fractions be identical as well?

    Mass fraction of a component is defined as mfi​=mmix​mi​​. Since total mass
    of the mixture is constant, and each gas has identical mass, mass fraction
    is identical for all gases.

    Mole fraction of a component is defined as yi​=Nmix​Ni​​.

    Expressing mass fraction in terms of molar masses,

    mfi​=mmix​mi​​=Nmix​Mmix​Ni​Mi​​=yi​Mmix​Mi​​

    yi​=mfi​Mi​Mmix​​

    From observation, since mfi​ and Mmix​ are constants, mole fraction will
    only be identical if the gases have identical molar masses Mi​. Otherwise,
    mole fraction will differ for each gas.

    #Part (d)

    Specific humidity is defined as ω=ma​mv​​. Since the container is sealed, there
    will be no change in masses of water vapor and dry air, thus ω is constant.
    From the figure, the process is represented by a horizontal line.

    Relative humidity is defined as ϕ=Pg​Pv​​=Psat@T​Pv​​. From first law for closed systems,
    heat input into the container will increase the air temperature. Air at a higher temperature will have a higher saturation pressure. Thus, ϕ will decrease.

    From the figure, the horizontal line cuts across decreasing ϕ lines. Hence, as
    the air is heated, relative humidity will decrease, corresponding to the result
    obtained from the equation.

    #Part (e)

    Combustion with 120% theoretical air as it has the least amount of excess air
    at 20%, as compared to the other cases, which are more than 20% excess air.

    #Part (f)

    #Part (i) + Part (ii)

    Balancing the chemical equation,

    CO+4O2​→CO2​+3.5O2​

    Using ideal gas law,

    PV=mRT

    PV=Nmix​Mmix​Rmix​T

    PV=Nmix​Ru​T

    Volume of tank,

    V=P1​Nmix​Ru​T1​​

    V=100(1+4)(8.314)(25+273)​

    V=123.8786 m3

    Final pressure in the tank,

    P2​=123.8786(1+3.5)(8.314)(227+273)​

    P2​=151 kPa

    P2​=1.51 atm

    Note that mole number of the final mixture differs from the initial mixture.

    #Part (iii)

    Using first law for combustion,

    Q=∑N(hˉf°​+hˉ−hˉ°)prod​−∑N(hˉf°​+hˉ−hˉ°)react​

    Q=N(hˉf°​+hˉ−hˉ°)CO2​​+N(hˉ−hˉ°)O2​​−N(hˉf°​)CO​

    Note that Δhˉ for reactants is zero as reactants are at the reference state.

    From Table 9,

    (hˉf°​)CO2​​=−393520 kJ/kmol

    (hˉf°​)CO​=−110530 kJ/kmol

    From property tables, at T1​=298 K,

    (hˉ°)CO2​​=9364 kJ/kmol

    (hˉ°)O2​​=8682 kJ/kmol

    From property tables, at T2​=500 K,

    (hˉ)CO2​​=17678 kJ/kmol

    (hˉ)O2​​=14770 kJ/kmol

    Substituting into the equation,

    Q=(−393520+17678−9364)+3.5(14770−8682)−(−110530)

    Q=−253368 kJ/kmol

    #Part (iv)

    Assumptions:

    • Cold-air standard: constant specific heats at room temperature 25°C
    • Combustion process is adiabatic
